label: Proposition J
title: Removal of Foreclosure Exemption for Real Property Transfer Tax
q: Shall the City permanently apply a transfer tax of between 0.5% and 6% of a property’s fair market value, on the transfer of properties such as commercial, industrial, and large residential properties, that are transferred to a lender because of foreclosure or to avoid foreclosure, for estimated annual revenue of $100 million to $150 million?
now: When a lender takes a property through foreclosure, it pays transfer tax only on what the property sold for above the unpaid debt.${F(1)}
does: Starting March 1, 2027, taxes those transfers on full market value, except homes and buildings with fewer than five units.${F(1)}
yes: You want lenders that take larger properties through foreclosure to pay the transfer tax on full value.${F(1)}
no: You don't want to make these changes.${F(1)}
intro: [warm] Before we dive in, where do you stand on Proposition J right now?

lwv.n: League of Women Voters of SF

y1.s: Supporters say a tax break meant for struggling homeowners now goes to corporate lenders that take office towers and big apartment buildings.
g: The tax they skip is the one every ordinary buyer pays
end exemption to real estate transfer tax by banks foreclosing on properties
src: "But the same tax break is also being given to financial institutions and corporate lenders when they acquire office towers, mega apartment complexes, and industrial buildings through foreclosure."
"Since 2023, 600 claims have been filed: only 23% were for single-family homes, 56% were for properties valued over $10 million, and less than 10% followed the conventional foreclosure pattern."
y1.fig: The pamphlet gives no count of claims. SPUR, citing the Assessor-Recorder, says investors avoided more than $450 million in transfer tax from 2023 to 2025. When the break began: proponents say 1984, GrowSF says 1967 and rewritten in 1984. Unverified.
resp: "The original 1984 tax rules were designed to keep the real estate market functioning during crises."

y2.s: Supporters say it would raise $100 million to $150 million a year for city services while the City faces a budget shortfall.
src: "Our city is dealing with a budget shortfall, and we are facing cuts to city services. Prop J helps close that gap"
"The measure could bring an average of $100 million to $150 million annually over the first five years."
y2.fig: Had it applied in the year ending June 2022, it would have raised $3.2 million. In the year ending June 2026, $232.5 million. The Controller expects revenue to be "highest in the near term then decline significantly over time."
resp: "What they fail to mention is that this money has no strings attached."

y3.s: Supporters say the tax falls on lenders taking big buildings, and leaves families who lose a home alone.
g: without harming individual homeowners or small landlords
src: "Prop J doesn’t touch families losing their homes."

A "qualified residential property" keeps the break: "a single-family residence, condominium, cooperative unit, single live/work unit, multifamily residential property with fewer than five residential units, or mixed-use property with fewer than five residential units and only a single floor of non-residential space."
y3.fig: None on how many homes are affected. A building with any unit for travelers or vacationers loses the break.
resp: "When lenders face higher operational costs, those costs are inevitably passed down to everyday San Franciscans through higher interest rates, stricter lending requirements, and reduced access to capital for local projects."

n1.s: Opponents say no other major California city taxes these transfers, so lenders would charge more to lend in San Francisco.
src: "No other major city in California imposes transfer taxes on distressed lenders taking back collateral."
"Lenders will respond by raising interest rates, demanding higher down payments, or avoiding San Francisco real estate entirely."
n1.fig: None in the pamphlet on interest rates. SPUR says San José and Oakland also exempt these transfers, and a measure on Oakland's November ballot would limit its exemption. In GrowSF's own worst case, not the Controller's, a $100 million office loan would cost about 0.14% more a year.
resp: "Investment firms and corporate lenders that foreclose on large commercial properties are sophisticated players who already price risk into every deal."

n2.s: Opponents say tax bills on distressed buildings would push them into fire sales or leave them empty, slowing downtown's recovery.
g: squeezes property owners at their most vulnerable moment
src: "When distressed properties face massive tax bills just to clear bad debt, lenders and property owners will be forced into drawn-out legal battles or distressed fire sales."
"San Francisco is already suffering from record-high commercial vacancies."
n2.fig: None in the pamphlet on vacancies or sale prices. SPUR, which backs J, lists the same risk as a con: "making it more expensive to buy and sell commercial real estate may slow its recovery."
resp: "The foreclosure tax will apply to office towers, industrial buildings, and mega-complexes that already exist, not new housing construction."

n3.s: Opponents call it a blank check for City Hall, and the Controller says some years it may bring in next to nothing.
src: "Don’t give City Hall another blank check while stalling our economic recovery."
"There may be years where the proposed measure generates next to no new tax revenue."
n3.fig: The money goes into the City's main budget, "to be expended for any City purpose." The Controller expects foreclosures to fall back to non-crisis levels within four to six years. If Proposition I, another measure on this ballot, also passes, GrowSF and SPUR say part of the money would go to its housing fund.
resp: "Keep an unfair corporate tax break meant for families. Or put millions of dollars back into our fund for city services."

y1: SPUR reports that 56% of exemption claims since 2023 were for properties over $10 million, up from 4% from 2008 to 2023. Opponents say the 1984 rules were meant to keep the market working in a crisis.
y2: Had it applied in the year ending June 2026, it would have raised $232.5 million, and in the year ending June 2022, $3.2 million. The Controller expects the most revenue early, then a steep decline.
y3: The break stays for houses, condos, co-ops and buildings with fewer than five homes. Foreclosed offices, shops, hotels and larger apartment buildings would be taxed on full market value.
n1: SPUR says San José and Oakland also exempt these transfers. In GrowSF's own worst case, a $100 million office loan would cost about 0.14% more a year.
n2: The pamphlet has no figure for fire sales or vacancies. SPUR, which supports J, lists slower commercial recovery as a con.
n3: The money goes into the City's main budget, for any City purpose. If Proposition I, another measure on this ballot, also passes, GrowSF says roughly half would go to its housing fund instead.

ORG.q: Proposition J is the kind of progressive, equitable, and necessary taxation the League of Women Voters supports.
Closing the foreclosure loophole for commercial and multi-family residential properties offers a way to increase revenue without harming individual homeowners or small landlords.
The tax they skip is the one every ordinary buyer pays, and homes and small buildings keep the exemption either way.
end exemption to real estate transfer tax by banks foreclosing on properties
Still, to make up some of that revenue, Mahmood suggesting eliminating the current tax exemption for buildings in foreclosure. Nothing wrong with that
Removes a longstanding tax exemption and squeezes property owners at their most vulnerable moment.
